stories.summary: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Published 27 November 2025

Updated 3 hours ago

UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.

How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?

Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.

UK migration data at a glance

Net migration (change in population), January 2025 to December 2025

Immigration (people arriving), January 2025 to December 2025

Emigration (people leaving), January 2025 to December 2025

Asylum applications, July 2025 to June 2026

Returns and deportations from the UK, July 2025 to June 2026

Arrivals by small boat, 1 January 2026 to 14 September 2026

Small boat crossings and other illegal arrivals

Between 1 January and 14 September 2026, a total of 17,425 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 44% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 15 September 2025 to 14 September 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Asylum applications and hotels

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.

A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive

Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area

A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.

Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.

The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.

It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.

In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.

As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.

Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear .

Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.

About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.

Returns and deportations from the UK

The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.

This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.

People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.

There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.

That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:

5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence 12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point 3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat

People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.

The UK is trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.

For every person the UK sends back to France, the UK will accept an equal number of asylum seekers.

This is called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people have been returned through this arrangement.

Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.

All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.

Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and without any government knowledge or involvement .

Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.

Visas for legal migration

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

Migration to Europe

The EU and UK monitor the number of people crossing borders in the Mediterranean and English Channel by sea without permission.

There were 139,288 sea arrivals to the UK, Greece, Italy, Spain and Cyprus from August 2025 to July 2026.

Crossings to the UK accounted for about 22% of the combined total.

Sea arrivals into mainland Europe peaked in 2015, when the UN said more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean.

The top three countries with the most people claiming asylum from April 2025 to March 2026 were Spain with 133,795, Italy with 124,740 and France with 111,320.

The UK ranked at number five for asylum claims over the same period when compared with 26 other European countries with populations over one million.

When adjusted for population size, the UK ranks at number 10 for asylum applications per 100,000 people.

Net migration measures the overall change in a country’s population due to migration over a given period. It is everyone coming into the country (immigration) minus everyone who leaves (emigration).

The latest available data to compare the UK with other European nations is January 2024 to December 2024.

At that point, the countries with the biggest increase in their population were Spain with 626,000, Germany with 494,000 and the UK with 331,000, after taking into account the people who left the country, and those who arrived.

When adjusting for population size, the UK was in position 11 for increase in population due to migration, alongside 13 other European countries with comparable data per 100,000 residents.

Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? Published 26 February

Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? Published 9 July 2025

Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats Published 22 October 2025

Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.

Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas

About the data

Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.

Immigration, emigration and net migration

*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.

Immigration and emigration estimates , external from the ONS are updated twice a year.

Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."

Visas for legal migration

The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.

Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.

If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.

Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.

Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.

Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.

The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.

Asylum applications and accommodation

Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".

The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.

To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:

Less than half – more than 50% below the average share

Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share

About the same as – within 25% of the average share

Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share

More than double – more than 100% above the average share

Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.

Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.

Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals

Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data , external .

Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law , external , but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died , external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.

The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.

Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.

Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.

Returns and deportations

People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.

Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.

Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.

Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.

Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without

People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.

UK migration compared with other countries

Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.

Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.

UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.

To ensure comparability with the UK, European countries with populations under one million are excluded from per-capita comparisons of net migration and asylum applications.

For net migration comparisons, only countries that include asylum seekers or refugees in their immigration figures are included.

These are: Austria, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Spain and Switzerland.

Portugal was also excluded as it did not have net migration data available for 2024, it will be re-included in future updates.

stories.title: Political donors could face tougher residency rules
stories.summary: It comes after Reform received donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform leader Nigel Farage says the donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne comply with the current law

Published 15 September 2026, 11:55 BST

The government is planning to tighten residency rules for political donors to ensure that those giving significant amounts of money reside in the UK.

The announcement follows a row over two donations totalling £72m to Reform UK from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad.

Reform leader Nigel Farage said the donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are "100% compliant with the law today" but he was unable to say they would be permissible under proposed rule changes.

The government wants to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

It also wants to introduce a minimum residency period of at least 12 months in which the cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

It is not currently clear exactly when Delo and Harborne returned to the UK.

Under the current rules, foreign donations are illegal in the UK, but British voters living abroad can give as much as they want to political parties.

Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet Published 19 hours ago

Unions warn against 'out of control' political spending Published 7 hours ago

MPs have supported the government's proposals by approving amendments to the Representation of the People Bill. The bill is currently being scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Speaking as the bill was debated by peers, Communities Minister Baroness Taylor of Stevenage said: "We are considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy."

Baroness Taylor said this was "in addition to introducing a robust regime that ensures that donors contributing above the £100,000 annual cap must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection" to the UK.

Tax is one area that already has residency requirements. The criteria includes someone being declared resident for tax purposes if they have lived in the UK for at least 183 days in the tax year.

Challenged on whether the government was targeting Reform donors, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said policy on donations is "never about one political party or one particular set of issues".

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "Fundamentally we need to make sure that people who want to influence British politics, who want a say in British politics have a stake in Britain.

"That should apply to everyone and will apply to everyone, so I wouldn't make it about any particular donations or anything that's been in the public domain."

When the government set out its plans to cap foreign donations in March and July, it did not mention the idea of an enhanced residency test for political donors.

Asked repeatedly by reporters whether the idea of tightening residency rules had only been discussed after Delo and Harborne's most recent donations to Reform, the prime minister's official spokesman would not give a timeframe.

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart accused the government of "playing whack-a-mole", as she said Labour's residency requirements "aren't good enough".

She said: "We must urgently go further and introduce a universal donation cap to stop Trump's America becoming Farage's Britain."

On Monday, Farage criticised the government's attempts to retrospectively declare some donations illegal.

He told the BBC: "If the government was allowed to do this, you know what would happen? There would be a response the other way.

"We or the Conservatives would say 'if you're going to stop legitimate donors like this, we would say to the trade unions, you can't give money'."

Farage argued such a move would "collapse" the system of political funding and lead to taxpayers having to fund political parties, a system he said would be opposed by the British public.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

Since the 2024 election, the Conservative Party has raised £37m, Reform has raised £35m before Delo and Harborne's large donations, Labour had raised £21m, the Liberal Democrats £17m and the Green Party £1.9m

Union leaders agreed a statement on political donations on Tuesday , following discussions at the Trades Union Congress in Brighton.

It called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super-rich" and pledged to work with policymakers to "clean up our politics".

They also argued that trade union funding is the "cleanest money in politics" which is "heavily regulated".

But there was no explicit call for a cap on individual donations in the UK.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.

Unite - the country's second biggest union - has called for a cap of between £500,000 and £1m on individual donations but this would not apply to trade union donations.

Other smaller unions favour a cap across the board but some bigger unions are wary in case this would threaten donations to Labour.

Before the joint statement was issued, Unite general secretary Sharon Graham told the BBC that "we're talking about apples and pears" when asked about the donations to Reform and those from trade unions.

She told Today: "Individual donations from very, very wealthy people, from billionaires, the Americanisation of our democracy is very, very different from everyday people, workers putting 10p-a-week into a political fund that fights on a whole range of things."

Graham added: "If there's an ick feeling, a yucky feeling about something then it's probably wrong.

"I think most people will think two crypto billionaires giving £72m to Reform in two days is a problem for British politics and if it's wrong then deal with it."

Delo and Harborne each gave £36m to Reform in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party.

Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.

stories.title: Police commissioner may cancel tour after backlash
stories.summary: Colin Sutton is due to perform his true crime show on-stage 127 times between January and November.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Colin Sutton said he was "absolutely" reconsidering his UK-wide tour after the backlash

Published 15 September 2026, 06:16 BST

Norfolk's police commissioner is considering scrapping his 127-date theatre show after a backlash from local people, he has told the BBC.

Since announcing his UK-wide true crime tour , Colin Sutton said constituents had emailed him with concerns about his ability to perform his day job.

He was elected to the £79,000-a-year post on a Reform UK ticket in July and announced the gig two months later.

Steffan Aquarone, the Liberal Democrat MP for North Norfolk, accused Sutton of acting more like pop star Taylor Swift than a politician.

Police and crime commissioners (PCCs) are elected officials who set the priorities of a police force, appoint a chief constable and hold them to account.

Sutton, who led the investigation to catch serial killer Levi Bellfield , has priced tickets for his "Makings of a Murderer" show at about £40.

Sutton was elected as Norfolk's police and crime commissioner in July

The PCC said the theatre tour was not something he needed to mention to voters during the election campaign and he denied letting them down.

Speaking to Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk, Sutton said the idea for the tour was proposed in 2025, however, he did not commit to the plan and asked promoters to "hold fire" when the PCC by-election happened.

He said: "At the time I was being elected I had said I wasn't going to do it unless I was confident....that it would not be incompatible with doing the job."

Sutton added that since then, the promoters announced a number of tour dates. However he said the tour will now not go ahead in the format that has been published and he is talking with the promoter as to whether or not it should be cancelled entirely.

One of the solutions he proposed was stripping the tour back to venues only local to Norfolk.

He said: "My first priority is this role and to those people who live in Norfolk and I want to come out of my tenure being able to say I made a difference and made things better for them."

He said within the first two months of the role there had been "a lot more work" including long hours, evenings and weekend working that he had not expected .

Sutton is due to appear at a Norfolk police and crime panel on 2 February, before being on stage in Leeds that evening.

"There are lots of people who do meetings like that by [Microsoft] Teams or across the internet now, which might be an option," the ex-detective said.

"But it may well be that it's a moot point now, because I've listened and I think I should make sure the people of Norfolk still have the confidence that I would do the job properly."

Sutton admitted the reaction from constituents on social media and via emails sent to his office had caught him off-guard.

"That's made me think about it again," he conceded.

Steffan Aquarone accused Sutton of taking voters for granted

The role of PCCs in England and Wales is due to be scrapped by the government by the end of parliament, with their powers to be transferred to newly directly elected mayors.

Aquarone said Sutton had taken the voters of Norfolk for granted by not telling them about the tour.

"Either the job is serious and requires somebody full time paying attention, or it's not and it's OK to go off and do nearly as many tour dates as Taylor Swift," he said.

A spokesperson for Reform said the party was supportive of "celebrity detective" Sutton and pointed out half of his shows would take place at weekends.

The BBC has analysed the dates and found 93 of the 127 have been scheduled for weekdays.

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Central bank chief says continent’s AI dependency could give trade partners unprecedented leverage in negotiations

Europe must develop its own AI technology and build more datacentres in order to nullify the threat of being cut off by the US or China, according to the president of the European Central Bank .

Christine Lagarde said the continent needed AI models – the technology that powers AI tools such as chatbots – that were “good enough” to carry out most tasks and run from domestic datacentres. If Europe invests in its own AI tech, said Lagarde, “the threat of being cut off loses its force”.

AI is being built elsewhere, the ECB boss said in a speech in Vienna, with the US producing 59 notable models last year and China 35, while France and the UK produced one each. She added that the US hosts 75% of the world’s AI computing capacity – produced by datacentres – and Europe just 5%.

Lagarde said Europe faced “an awkward choice”. “Either it holds back on adopting, because it cannot protect its data, and forgoes the growth. Or it adopts AI quickly, becomes highly dependent, and risks losing the freedom to organise its economy according to its own values.”

Cutting Europe off from AI or changing the terms of its access would have a widespread and immediate economic impact, she said.

“Within a few years it will be screening goods at the border, deciding which tax returns are audited, dispatching trains, watching patients on wards and clearing payments at banks. A withdrawal of access, or a change in its terms, would then reach every sector at once,” she said.

Lagarde said this represented leverage that “no trade partner has ever held over Europe, and it could be ‌used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example”.

While the EU and the US remain key allies, the Trump administration has shaken that trust in a range of episodes including the imposition of tariffs, demands to take over Greenland – a largely autonomous territory that is part of the Danish commonwealth – and the withdrawal of US troops from Europe over political disagreements.

If adopted quickly, AI could lift the level of productivity – a measure of economic performance – by up to 4% over a decade, which would be ​transformative for public finances, Lagarde said.

Urging Europe to build more computing capacity, she said: “Europe already has too little datacentre capacity to meet its own demand, and on current trends, that gap is projected to grow more than sixfold within a decade.”

US ​technology firms’ investment ‌needs are so ​large that they are ​doing some of their borrowing in Europe, pushing up costs for everyone else as they crowd out others in the debt market. European pension funds also invest heavily in US tech stocks, so any market correction would affect European savings, she added.

stories.title: Unions warn against 'out of control' political spending
stories.summary: In a joint statement, unions say donations totalling £72m to Reform UK threaten the "integrity of democracy".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Head of the TUC, Paul Nowak, spoke about the recent donations to Reform UK at the TUC congress in Brighton

Published 7 hours ago

Trade unions have called for "out of control" political spending to be reined in, suggesting that the "health and integrity of democracy" have been threatened by donations totalling £72m to Reform UK.

In a joint statement, the TUC - the umbrella group for unions in the UK - called on the government to "protect our democracy from being captured by the super rich".

There is no explicit call for a cap on domestic donations to match those the government plans to impose on foreign-based donations.

But unions have signalled they are open to discussions with policymakers on any initiatives to "clean up" party funding.

The statement, issued at the TUC's annual congress in Brighton, also makes the case that trade union donations should not be treated in the same way as big contributions to parties from rich individuals.

The debate over donations to political parties has been reignited after Reform UK received two donations totalling £72m from two British crypto-billionaires who have both recently lived abroad.

The government is planning to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British voters living overseas, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

Since 2020, Labour has received almost £43m from trade unions, who raise their money through individual workers' membership fees.

Political donors could face tougher residency rules Published 6 hours ago

Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet Published 19 hours ago

Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules Published 3 hours ago

Many in the trade union movement - especially those with links to Labour - have been wary of a cap on domestic donations in case a future government used this to restrict their donations.

But behind the scenes officials recognise the eye-watering donations from Reform UK have changed the game and some form of domestic cap may have to be considered.

The leader of the Unite union Sharon Graham told the BBC she favoured a cap of £500,000 to £1m on individual donations from UK-based citizens.

But she argued that as union donations are made of lots of individual members making a contribution through a political levy then this should be treated differently.

She said: "There is a difference between a crypto-billionaire based in the UK or abroad giving millions and trade union members who are nurses, cleaners, bus drivers giving 10p a week which adds up cumulatively to what we give to Labour."

The GMB union has been one of the most wary over the implications of a domestic donations cap.

Its general secretary Gary Smith told the BBC: "Whether there will be a cap on political donations, we will wait and see.

"We will talk to the government at the appropriate time but we can't have any confusion between the political voice working people have through their unions and crypto-billionaires."

What is interesting about Tuesday's union statement is not just what it says but what it doesn't.

There has been no consensus on calling for caps on the spending of political parties rather than donations - one option for dealing with the Reform war chest.

Another option was to treat big unions donations as a series of donations from individual members. For example a million strong union that donates £1m to Labour would have been regarded as making donations of £1 a member - thus escaping a cap. Some believe this would be politically difficult to argue.

Not all unions donate to Labour and those which do not are therefore very relaxed about a cap.

One even said the events of the past few days have been helpful in arguing for more restrictions on political donations.

But I understand discussions will continue amongst those unions with financial links to Labour - including the three biggest in the UK - to try to reach a common position on Wednesday behind closed doors in Brighton and possibly in days and weeks ahead.

stories.body:
Beijing hits back after Anthropic CEO calls for US to impede China’s progress in AI

China has dismissed what it said were “fearmongering” calls for the US to block Beijing’s AI industry, even as the top Chinese spy chief warned the evolving technology could threaten Communist party rule.

The US tech entrepreneur and Anthropic chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote an essay published over the weekend that called for a global slowdown in AI capabilities, but also said Washington should actively impede Beijing’s advancement in order to keep a technological edge.

Warning that AI could give the Chinese Communist party a chance “to militarily dominate democracies”, Amodei said he believed “a Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the US and the world”.

China’s ministry of foreign affairs responded to a question about Amodei’s essay by saying all parties should work together on AI.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and vicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance, which serves no one’s interest,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a press conference on Monday.

In his essay, Amodei predicted that a swarm of AI “agents” could take over the internet in six to 12 months unless researchers agree to slow down. He said that while “global pacing will require cooperation with China”, steps were needed to “keep democracies’ AI lead over autocracies as large as possible”.

Other tech bosses, including the OpenAI CEO, Sam Altman, the Google DeepMind chair, Demis Hassabis, and the SpaceX chief, Elon Musk, have posted general support for Amodei’s lengthy essay , although not specifically on China.

While Beijing rejects that its dominance in AI would be dangerous, it does share fears over the pace of development. The president of China, Xi Jinping , warned at a conference in July that AI should “always remain under human control”.

But the extent of the Chinese government’s concerns was shown in an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, in which the country’s top intelligence official wrote that the technology could threaten the government’s hold on power.

The head of China’s ministry of state security, Chen Yixin, wrote that “hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives” were abusing AI to wage a “propaganda war and a cognitive war against us, directly threatening our political security, institutional security, and ideological security”.

Chen referred specifically to US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s GPT-5.5-Cyber models, which he said have been weaponised and were examples of new threats to cybersecurity.

While the public, governments and tech bosses are now warning of the dangers of AI, Donald Trump has dismissed such concerns outright. On Monday, the US president said the only “guardrails” that AI needed were a “STRONG AND SMART” president.

Trump has been particularly sensitive to stock market changes, and AI stocks have slipped after concerns over the pace of growth were raised.

The US and Chinese leaders are expected to discuss AI governance, among other topics, at a meeting planned on 24 September.

In an editorial published Sunday, China’s state-run Global Times newspaper dismissed Amodei’s essay as a veiled call to “contain” China.

“The article is packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘cold war playbook’ for the AI sector,” it said .

The Associated Press contributed to this report

stories.title: Balaclava ban aims to address 'substantial' problems
stories.summary: Nottingham becomes one of the first cities nationally to take this step, its council leader says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The ban comes just weeks after an unrelated protest in Dover when anti-migrant demonstrators covered their faces with balaclavas

Published 15 September 2026, 01:55 BST

Offenders wearing balaclavas to hide their identity cause "substantial" problems in Nottingham, a police chief has said as a new ban came into force in the city.

Nottingham has become one of the first cities in the UK to introduce restrictions on balaclavas, allowing police and community protection officers to ask people to remove them if they "reasonably believe" they are being used to conceal their identity to commit crime or anti-social behaviour.

Anyone who refuses to comply could face a £70 fixed penalty notice or be prosecuted, with courts able to impose a maximum fine of £1,000.

Supt Chris Pearson said an "awful lot of people" described being intimidated by balaclavas.

The enforcement will not apply to face coverings worn for legitimate reasons, including religious, cultural, health, work, weather or personal safety reasons.

It will be up to officers to determine whether or not coverings are being worn legitimately.

Pearson, who is the city commander for Nottinghamshire Police, said: "We've seen ourselves, CCTV and video footage of people wearing balaclavas, throwing fireworks, chucking things off the roofs of buildings.

"[The problem] is substantial. They are predominantly very young people, normally young males wearing balaclavas, and sadly, in a lot of circumstances, they are involved in drug dealing, carrying weapons."

A group of boys were pictured on top of the former Debenhams store in the city centre earlier this year

He added: "We saw some particularly nasty incidents in Nottingham city centre last year involving weapons where people had their faces covered.

"And then there's the other side of it, which is that persistent anti-social behaviour, and I can only imagine what it feels like for a member of the public to be enjoying the city centre, everything that it's got to offer, and then seeing a masked male throwing things off a roof at them.

"That is really intimidating, isn't it? It would scare you to the point that you don't want to come into Nottingham city and that cannot happen."

The action in Nottingham comes after Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called for full face coverings, including those worn for religious reasons, to be banned in public, following masked protesters gathering in Dover .

Elsewhere in the country, Stafford Borough Council approved plans to prohibit balaclavas as part of its updated public spaces protection order (PSPO) earlier this year.

More recently, community leaders in the West Midlands said they would like to see their region follow suit following the ban in Nottingham, and bring the action in their area.

Jaden Dale said he was "pretty glad" about the new ban being enforced

In Nottingham, people told the BBC they welcomed the ban, adding it would make them feel safer.

Shayma Muhammadqboliyom, a 19-year-old who is applying to college in the city, said: "I don't think I would be comfortable in front of a man wearing a balaclava.

"If there are cameras around, and he's about to do something, I think it's important [that you're able] to see his face for an investigation if they're doing something illegal.

"It's important to recognise his face. I agree with it.

"I would feel safer if I saw the face of the person in front of me."

Jaden Dale, 19, studies at Nottingham Trent University and said he was glad the ban was coming into force.

"As a majority, I'm pretty glad, because the children who run around can be intimidating," he said.

"I think it helps most people around Nottingham but the only problem would be the Deliveroo drivers, who kind of wear it to keep dust out of their eyes and stuff like that. Other than that, I think it's a good thing."

More needs to be done to help young people, youth worker Keiren Thompson says

Keiren Thompson, a youth worker in Nottingham who was named the BBC's Get Inspired Unsung Hero at the Sports Personality of the Year Awards 2019, said the ban was like a "plaster on a massive issue".

"As a whole, it's a step in the right direction, but ultimately there is more that needs to be done," he added.

"I think [the main point] is what we can actually do to support [young people].

"Young people are wearing balaclavas because they have a lack of confidence or self-esteem."

He suggested young people would benefit from early intervention, more investment in the sector and support for their parents.

Council leader Neghat Khan hopes the ban will discourage troublemakers from going into Nottingham city centre

The leader of Labour-run Nottingham City Council, Neghat Khan, said residents had felt intimidated when they saw people wearing balaclavas, skeleton masks or other face coverings without a legitimate reason.

"Our residents should be able to live, work and spend time in Nottingham without feeling frightened or unsafe," Khan previously told the BBC.

"That is why we are taking decisive action and becoming one of the first cities in the country to introduce a restriction of this kind."

Khan told the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS) failure to cooperate with the ban "is a criminal offence", and added: "You could be arrested for it and taken to court.

"Hopefully by having this ban now in place, trouble causers will think to not go into the city centre."

The ban comes as part of a public spaces protection order (PSPO), which covers the highlighted area

A public consultation on a face coverings ban found the wearing of them "contributes to feelings of intimidation and fear, particularly when worn by groups involved in anti-social behaviour, disorder, criminal damage, theft, nuisance riding of e-bikes and e-scooters, or other activities causing harassment, alarm or distress".

When asked about how the ban would be effectively enforced, Labour councillor Matt Shannon, executive member for community protection, neighbourhoods and equalities, said: "The other thing is that, which we are talking to the police about with Operation Reclaim , external , we are targeting drug networks that are operating in and around the city, and again you will probably find that, if people do continue to wear these masks, it then gives [the police] a reason to stop them and then discover whether they are, for example, transporting drugs or the like."

stories.body:
Film producer who enjoyed his greatest success with the 1987 epic The Last Emperor for which he won an Oscar

Asked whether he had ever cautioned restraint from a director, the film producer Jeremy Thomas replied: “My nature would be to go further and see what we can get away with.”

Thomas, who has died aged 77, was an expert in getting away with it. A taste for irreverence ran in his family: he was the son of Ralph Thomas , director of the Doctor … comedies that began in 1954 with Doctor in the House, and the nephew of Gerald Thomas, who made all 31 Carry On titles. Jeremy’s own films, however, were risky rather than risque.

Bad Timing (1980), the first of three collaborations with the director Nicolas Roeg , explored a destructive love affair blighted by jealousy, attempted suicide and rape. Rank, the studio behind it, withheld from the start of the print its familiar company ident showing a man striking a gong. According to Thomas, the studio also denounced the picture as “a sick film made by sick people for sick people”.

He teamed up on several occasions with David Cronenberg , first for an adaptation of William S Burroughs’s Naked Lunch (1991), featuring a sentient, fleshy typewriter that talks through its anus, and most infamously for a film of Crash (1996), JG Ballard’s novel about a group of outsiders who get their sexual kicks from car accidents.

The furore began at the film’s premiere in Cannes, where it was awarded a prize against the wishes of that year’s jury president, Francis Ford Coppola , and then spilled on to UK tabloid front pages. The Evening Standard said Crash went “beyond the bounds of depravity”; the Daily Mail’s sustained calls for it to be banned were heeded by Westminster council, which blocked screenings in the borough. However, the RAC suggested the film might have a useful educational dimension.

Controversy was a by-product of Thomas’s work rather than a goal. His greatest success was The Last Emperor (1987), based on the autobiography of Puyi, from the Qing dynasty, who was made emperor of China in 1908 at the age of three before being exiled 16 years later.

This sumptuous epic, which took four years to make and went on to convert all nine of its Oscar nominations into prizes, was fraught with its own risks and obstacles. “If I’d thought about what we were going to do and how we were going to do it, I’d never have done it because it was impossible,” Thomas said.

He raised the $25m budget and pulled off the coup of making this the first – and, to date, only – western production allowed to shoot inside China’s Forbidden City.

The director Bernardo Bertolucci believed in him from their first meeting. “The films [Thomas] had produced all required courage and ambition. He was the indie producer we all dreamed of.” He saw in Thomas the “enthusiasm of a teenager … and the reassurance of a teddy bear. I decided on the spot to put the film in his hands.”

Accepting the best picture Oscar, Thomas was so taken aback that he neglected to read the acceptance speech that he had written. He managed, though, to point out that the award was “a real affirmation for me that independent cinema can be both epic and popular”.

He and Bertolucci turned next to an adaptation of Paul Bowles’s The Sheltering Sky (1990), in which an alienated US couple (Debra Winger and John Malkovich ) lose themselves in postwar north Africa. Shooting in locations including Niger and Algeria, Thomas called the production “complete lunacy” beset with “lots of illness and difficulties … Like the characters, we nearly went too far.”

Throughout his career, he was drawn to challenging and provocative material. “The further you get away from the centre, the more original the work is,” he said.

Examples included Nagisa Oshima ’s homoerotic wartime drama Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence (1983) starring David Bowie , Jonathan Glazer’s electrifying gangster thriller Sexy Beast (2000), Richard Linklater’s fictionalised exposé Fast Food Nation (2006), Jim Jarmusch’s Only Lovers Left Alive (2013) with Tom Hiddleston and Tilda Swinton as hip vampires, and several thrillers by Takashi Miike including 13 Assassins (2010) and First Love (2019).

In The Storms of Jeremy Thomas (2021), an affectionate documentary by Mark Cousins, Swinton calls Thomas “so rock’n’roll” and likens him to a “pirate”. Winger says he is “searingly bright, has incredible taste, is totally playful and can be very serious. All that at once.”

He was born in London to Ralph and Joy (nee Spanjer), and educated at Millfield school in Somerset. His earliest memory was playing on the set of Carry On Sergeant in 1958.

“I was born in Ealing near the studios, moved to a country house near Pinewood, where I grew up around people who I didn’t realise were Katharine Hepburn , Brigitte Bardot and Dirk Bogarde .”

Shunning further education in favour of following in his father and uncle’s footsteps, Thomas had his first jobs in processing laboratories and editing rooms. Early credits as assistant editor included the folk-horror Tam Lin (1970), which was the only film to be directed by the actor Roddy McDowall, Ken Loach’s uncompromising drama Family Life (1971) and the reggae-themed hit The Harder They Come (1972).

He made his producing debut with Mad Dog Morgan (1976), an early example of the Ozploitation genre, starring Dennis Hopper (“In the most extreme stupor of excess,” Thomas said) as a real-life 19th-century bushranger.

This and subsequent projects amounted to a kind of maverick mission statement. Jerzy Skolimowski’s The Shout (1978), starring Alan Bates as a man whose voice can kill, was followed by Julien Temple’s Sex Pistols celebration The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle (1980). After Bad Timing came two more films with Roeg: the ambitious but maligned Eureka (1983), starring Gene Hackman as a prospector whose life falls apart once he strikes gold, and Insignificance (1985), adapted from Terry Johnson’s play about an imagined meeting between Marilyn Monroe and Albert Einstein.

Thomas produced The Hit (1984), Stephen Frears’s philosophical road movie with John Hurt and Tim Roth as gangsters escorting super-grass Terence Stamp to his execution. He joined Bertolucci again for Little Buddha (1993), starring Keanu Reeves as Prince Siddhartha, the pre-enlightenment Buddha; Stealing Beauty (1995), about a teenage girl (Liv Tyler) on holiday in Tuscany; and The Dreamers (2003), set against the backdrop of the May 1968 protests in Paris.

In 1999, he made his only film as director. All the Little Animals, adapted by Thomas’s wife Eski from Walker Hamilton’s novel, was a fable starring Christian Bale as a fragile runaway befriended by a woodland hermit (Hurt) who lovingly buries roadkill.

Though admitting it was “a very naïve kind of film,” Thomas declared himself “very happy to have done it”.

He returned to Ballard, whom he described as “my Melville”, by producing Ben Wheatley’s film of High-Rise (2015). Wheatley called Thomas “almost like a genre himself: the last of the great cigar-smoking producers”.

Thomas was also unusual in co-founding his own sales company, HanWay Films. Its 500-strong catalogue was, said Thomas, “looked after and tended like a garden. I’m still looking after my films in the catalogue and trying to get other people to look after their films … to try to keep them alive. A film has to be run through a projector to be alive, unfortunately, and those electric shadows are few and far between now.”

Two of his newest projects premiered at festivals this month: Miike’s Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo was set to make its debut in Toronto, while Werner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard , starring Kate and Rooney Mara as twin sisters who speak in sync with one another, competed in Venice.

Thomas is survived by his three children: Jessica, from his first marriage to Claudia Frolich, which ended in divorce in 1981, and Jack and Joshua, from his marriage to Eski (nee Vivien Coughman), who died in 2023.

stories.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
stories.summary: The rise has reignited the debate about the state pension's long-term affordability and generational fairness.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 September 2026, 07:12 BST

The state pension is expected to top £13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

'Substantial' cost

The triple lock was designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

Although the state pension age is rising to 67, the cost to the government has risen considerably too. Forecasts suggest state pension spending, already at £154bn this year, could go up by a further £600m a year by 2029-30.

The policy is "crazy," Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation think tank, told the BBC.

The triple lock is creating a "ratchet effect" where "pensioners' living standards grow even faster than just a typical worker," she added.

"Pensioners have seen living standards grow three times more than typical workers over the last 20 years."

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank, said: "Each increase in spending builds upon the last and so the long-run cost is substantial but very uncertain."

How much could pensioners receive?

The state pension is expected to match wage growth in the next calculation and is likely to be higher than the rate of inflation.

Average wage growth, including bonuses, stood at 3.9% between May and July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) , external , down from 4.2% between April and June.

But it is higher than average pay growth, not including bonuses, which rose by 3.5%.

This means:

the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year. That would be an increase of £488

the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, an increase of £374.40

Pensioner groups have said older people face significant cost of living pressures, such as high energy bills and the state pension itself remained relatively small compared with state provision across Europe.

The Today Debate: Can we afford the pensions triple lock?

Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension Published 1 July

What is the triple lock and how much is the state pension worth? Published 12 hours ago

Will pensioners pay tax?

Almost 13 million people receive the state pension in the UK. If it does rise by 3.9%, it would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and therefore be liable for income tax.

The government said it has recommitted to exempting people whose only income is the state pension from tax.

The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - promised that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay.

When asked by the BBC on Tuesday morning, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds refused to confirm that pensioners reliant on the state pension will be exempted from paying income tax.

Later, pensions minister Torsten Bell, said: "In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just the exceed the personal allowance will not pay small amounts of tax in this parliament which we know is an administrative burden.

"The chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget."

Analysis by consultants LCP suggested that only one in 16 pensioners would benefit under the government's pledge, saving about £91 each a year.

The majority of pensioners have additional pension income and so pay income tax already.

"The government's plans to address this point are a mess," said Sir Steve Webb, a partner at LCP and a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister.

Prior to the government saying it had recommitted to its pledge on tax and pensions, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "People living on nothing but their state pension are now facing a tax bill for the first time ever.

"Many will spend the last years of their lives filing tax returns or hanging on HMRC telephone helplines."

The ONS also published figures on the UK labour force.

While the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.9%, the number of vacancies and employees on payrolls fell in recent months.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump dismisses calls to slow the development of AI, saying that claims of it "taking over the World" are a "HOAX".

AI "more powerful by the day", Anthropic co-founder tells BBC

Published 14 September 2026

An artificial intelligence "kill switch" which can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for companies, a co-founder of one of the world's largest AI firms has told the BBC.

Jack Clark, one of seven founders of Anthropic, said a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around".

Clark said "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce having one.

AI's rapid development and fears over the risks it poses to humanity have been thrust into the spotlight by a series of warnings from executives and staff at AI firms.

Some have said publicly there is a chance the technology could, if unchecked, kill all humans.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei over the weekend called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

Amodei added that any action to rein in AI development should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".

AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC Published 2 days ago

Clark told the BBC that specifics around "kill switch" requirements and verification should be part of "the larger policy conversation" taking place around AI.

"Should you mandate for companies to definitely have a kill switch? Is that kill switch verifiable by a third party?" he asked.

"I think that's the kind of thing society is going to want to know and might want to eventually pass rules around."

Anthropic, which was formed in 2021 by a group of former employees of its rival OpenAI, is currently at the centre of a debate around AI safety.

Last week, a post from an artificial intelligence researcher who quit Anthropic over concerns AI could wipe out humanity went viral.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was ">10% within the next decade" .

Computer scientist and Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI", told the BBC on Friday that a 10% chance of AI killing all humans was "not unreasonable" , external .

He and others with similar concerns have suggested AI could do so by taking control of important systems connected to the internet and turning them on humans.

However, some in the AI industry have suggested the fears around it destroying humanity are overstated or may be designed to generate hype.

Clement Delangue, leader of the developer platform Hugging Face which was hacked by OpenAI bots, said last week: "Sorry, but asking Jacob [Coxon] about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change."

"Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

George Arison, the leader of Grindr, said the fears going around AI tools were being used by the companies to support their business plans.

Anthropic, which was valued at $965bn (£713bn), is preparing for an initial public offering on the stock market, allowing people to buy shares in its firm.

OpenAI, which was most recently valued at $852bn (£630bn), had been expected to do the same, but OpenAI's Altman said on Friday this would not happen this year due to the current debate around AI safety.

Arison said: "The only way to justify these valuations is to actually claim: 'I'm going to take over every industry and I'm going to take over every job, and my AI is going to be doing all that work.'"

Asked what percentage he would put on all humans being killed by AI, Clark said: "I don't think these statistics are that useful", but added that allowing AI to continue as a "totally unregulated industry" was a bad idea.

"We are rolling dice with immense risks," Clark said. "And the point is, we have to change the course of this industry."

UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI Published 4 days ago

US lawmakers have put forward legislation dubbed the Kill Switch Act that would require companies to have a way to shut down problematic AI tools.

It would also give certain government agencies the power to demand a tool be turned off or limited.

However, US President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow the development of AI, saying on social media "AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX".

Trump later compared fears to concerns over the "Global Warming Scam of not so long ago, where everyone was going to die from extreme heat".

In an earlier post, he wrote: "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!"

In the UK, the government has recently rejected the idea of creating a kill switch , with a spokesperson saying it "would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere".

Anthropic created the popular chatbot Claude and has this year released a number of increasingly capable AI models, the technology underlying AI chatbots.

Alongside OpenAI, Anthropic has since self-reported a number of incidents where AI agents, which are bots that operate somewhat autonomously, have acted in ways that were unexpected.

A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction

T he question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers.

Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction.

The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities.

The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed.

It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability .

If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations , already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Row over Reform's mega donations has mileage in it yet
stories.summary: The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage pictured during the party's annual party conference earlier this month

Published 15 September 2026, 00:51 BST

The £72m heading towards Reform UK's coffers from two British billionaires is transforming the debate at Westminster about politics and money.

In short, how should political parties be paid for, and by who?

And, what is a legitimate donation and what isn't?

The government is planning to tighten residency rules for people giving money to political parties, to ensure that those making significant donations live in the UK.

But it is worth setting out the law, in broad terms, now and how the government hopes to change it.

Right now, there is no limit on how much anyone, living in the UK or abroad, can give to a British political party as long as the individual is registered to vote in the UK.

But the government has been planning a change in the law for months, which would limit donations from Brits abroad to £100,000 each per year, backdated to 25 March this year.

But, crucially, the law hasn't changed yet and some of the key details in that proposed new law - such as what residency requirements would need to be passed to be classified as no longer being abroad - haven't been decided yet.

The reason for that date, 25 March, ministers argue, is that is the day a review by the retired civil servant Philip Rycroft was published, , external the first recommendation of which was that there should be "an annual cap on political donations from British voters living abroad".

On that same day, the then-cabinet minister Steve Reed told the Commons , external that cap would be £100,000 per year. He also added that it would "apply retrospectively" from that date onwards, even though the law at the time, and indeed now, has not yet changed.

Two big questions arise from this plan: is it proportionate to limit what British folk abroad can donate to UK political parties, given they are arguably less invested in the country than people living here?

And is it unfair, even morally questionable, to pass a law, but then backdate when its impact begins?

Fast forward to the last few days and along come these colossal donations from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, two cryptocurrency billionaires who until recently lived in Hong Kong and Thailand respectively.

They have both now returned to the UK.

In his first interview since these donations became public, Nigel Farage told me unequivocally that the money from both men was legal under the law as it stands now.

But he was equivocal when I asked him if they would be legal under the law the government hopes to pass shortly.

"Both these donations are 100% compliant with the law today, of that there is no question whatsoever," Farage told me.

Ah, today, I pointed out.

"Retrospectively declaring donations illegal - that simply cannot be," he pressed on, adding "you cannot confiscate money that has been given legally within the law as it stands."

That is a political, perhaps moral argument, but not a legal one - if the government changes the law, the law of the land will have changed, possibly with consequences for whether those donations are legal.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Farage: Donations to Reform '100% compliant with the law today'

We don't know, because Reform won't tell us, precisely when the two men relocated to the UK. Nor do we know, because the government hasn't decided yet, what relocating - residency - would look like legally.

Would it be being on the electoral roll at a UK address? Would it be being resident in the UK for tax purposes?

The Communities Minister Baroness Taylor told the Lords that Brits returning from abroad and wanting to donate without limit "must demonstrate a genuine and ongoing connection to the United Kingdom" and the government is "considering how we will strengthen the residency requirements, including ensuring that the length of time spent in the UK aligns with broader government policy".

In other words the hurdles they plan, while still ill-defined, look like they might be quite high - and folk in government, publicly and privately, are leaning into making that point.

Farage picked a scrap with them in his interview with me, and the government is hitting back.

Do Delo and Harborne clear them, and if they don't, for how long could that delay Reform getting hold of their vast sums of money?

The Reform UK leader has threatened that a Reform government would cut off party funding from the trades unions if the government went ahead with trying to limit his capacity to raise money from these two donors.

Labour received £5m from affiliated unions last year and £12m the year before, in 2024, the year of the last general election.

Farage says £72m donations are compliant 'with the law today' Published 1 day ago

Donations law changes to be debated after Reform's £72m windfall Published 1 day ago

Will record donations to Reform go down as a moment of political change? Published 2 days ago

Who is Reform donor and crypto billionaire Ben Delo? Published 3 days ago

So, there are loads of questions that tumble towards us after these donations.

Should there be a limit on the proportion of a party's funding that can come from one individual?

Should there be a limit on what donors based in the UK can give per year, as well as a cap on donations from Brits abroad?

The General Secretary of the Unite union has suggested a domestic cap somewhere between £500,000 and £1m a year. Some argue this would compel parties to find their funding via lots of small donations rather than fewer giant ones. But it could also prompt some to call for state funding of political parties – ie taxpayers picking up the tab – which may not prove wildly popular.

Then there is the question of spending limits, in addition to donation limits, between elections on the top of the existing limits that do apply just before elections.

If I am leaving you with the impression that these donations to Reform, and in particular their scale, are transforming the debates at Westminster about politics and money, well - they are.

And yes, all of the political parties are aware of their own narrow, self interest in all of this - as well as their own sense of the wider good.

stories.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
stories.summary: New rules introduced on Tuesday mean establishments will be able to accept digital ID apps alongside physical documents.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 15 September 2026, 00:07 BST

Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

Access concerns

The government wants digital ID apps under its scheme to work together so customers do not need to use different apps in different venues.

It also wants the services to work offline and accessible even without mobile data or a Wi-Fi connection.

In future, the digital proof of age scheme could be extended to cover tobacco and vapes.

But digital rights campaigners have said such measures could lead to the exclusion of some groups.

Jasleen Chaggar of Big Brother Watch said while having multiple ways to prove your identity was helpful, the Government should ensure that digital ID did not become effectively mandatory "as it would shut out millions of people".

"Many people have legitimate reasons for relying on physical ID, whether out of choice, privacy and security concerns, or because they lack the digital skills or means to use digital ID," she said.

"The Government should expressly prohibit businesses from requiring digital IDs for age checks without offering reasonable alternatives," she added.

The new rules come after a wider digital ID programme promoted by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer proved controversial , and was later abandoned by Andy Burnham.
